blocks.recap_md: Passing procedures as arguments already added expressive power; returning procedures as values adds even more - motivated by revisiting the fixed-point square-root idea and generalizing average damping into its own reusable procedure.
`average-damp` takes a procedure `f` and returns a new procedure that, applied to `x`, gives the average of `x` and `(f x)` - applying it to `square` at 10 averages 10 and 100 to get 55.

`sqrt` is rewritten using `fixed-point` plus `average-damp` applied to `y -> x/y`, making fixed-point search, damping, and the transform all explicit - and the same pattern immediately generalizes to `cube-root` by damping `y -> x/y^2` instead.

Square roots were already a special case of Newton's method: a zero of a differentiable function g is a fixed point of x - g(x)/Dg(x), and this fixed-point search converges rapidly given a good initial guess.
Derivative is introduced as another function-to-function transform, and `deriv` approximates it via a small increment `dx` (defined here as 0.00001) rather than symbolic differentiation.
Like `average-damp`, `deriv` takes a procedure and returns a procedure; applying it to `cube` approximates the derivative of x^3 at 5, landing very close to the exact value 75.
`newton-transform` packages the Newton's-method formula using `deriv`, and `newtons-method` is simply `fixed-point` applied to that transform, starting from a supplied guess.
Applying `newtons-method` to y^2 - x with an initial guess of 1 gives yet a third way of defining `sqrt`.

Both routes to `sqrt` share the same shape - start from a function, transform it, then find a fixed point - so that shape is factored out into a general `fixed-point-of-transform` procedure taking a function, a transform, and a guess.
The two earlier `sqrt` formulations become two calls to the same `fixed-point-of-transform` procedure, one passing `average-damp` and one passing `newton-transform`.

Compound procedures already let us name general methods explicitly; higher-order procedures let us manipulate those methods further, which connects to first-class status - the freedom to be named, passed, returned, and stored - that Lisp grants procedures fully, unlike many other languages.
Exercises invite defining `cubic` for use with `newtons-method`, `double` for applying a procedure twice, and `compose` for composing two one-argument functions.

Remaining exercises cover `repeated` (applying a function n times), smoothing a function via averaging nearby outputs, experimenting with how many average-damps an n-th-root fixed-point search needs, and `iterative-improve` as the general guess-and-improve pattern.

knowledge_items.statement: `average-damp` is a higher-order procedure: given a procedure `f`, it returns a new procedure that, applied to `x`, produces the average of `x` and `(f x)` - a reusable transform for taming fixed-point iterations that would otherwise oscillate or fail to converge.

`sqrt` and `cube-root` can both be derived as fixed-point searches of an average-damped transform, differing only in which function of y is being damped (y -> x/y for square root, y -> x/y^2 for cube root) - making the shared structure explicit and reusable.

`deriv` approximates the derivative of a function g at a point by computing (g(x+dx) - g(x))/dx for a small constant dx; like `average-damp`, it takes a procedure as argument and returns a procedure as its value.

Newton's method finds a zero of g by treating it as a fixed-point search of the transform x -> x - g(x)/Dg(x); `newton-transform` builds this transform using `deriv`, and `newtons-method` is just `fixed-point` applied to that transform - yielding a third formulation of `sqrt`.

Since both the average-damping route and the Newton's-method route to `sqrt` share the same shape (transform a function, then find its fixed point), that shape is abstracted into `fixed-point-of-transform`, so the two `sqrt` definitions become two instantiations of one general procedure differing only in the transform argument passed.

Higher-order procedures like `average-damp`, `deriv`, and `fixed-point-of-transform` let a programmer name and manipulate entire general methods of computation as explicit elements of the language, not just parameterize over ordinary numeric values.

An element has first-class status if it may be named by variables, passed as an argument, returned as a result, and included in data structures; Lisp grants procedures full first-class status, unlike many other common programming languages, which greatly increases expressive power at some implementation cost.

questions.prompt: What does `(average-damp f)` return, given a procedure `f`?
options: A new procedure that, when applied to x, returns the average of x and (f x)
A new procedure that returns the average of two successive outputs of f
The average of f applied to every number from 1 up to x
A number equal to the average of f's minimum and maximum output values
questions.explanation: average-damp packages exactly this transform - a lambda over x that computes the average of x and (f x) - converting f into a 'damped' version of itself, which is what tames fixed-point iterations that would otherwise oscillate.

questions.prompt: Why can `cube-root` be written by making only a small change to the fixed-point/average-damp formulation of `sqrt`?
options: Because the cube root of x is a fixed point of y -> x/y^2, just as the square root of x is a fixed point of y -> x/y, so only the inner transform function needs to change
Because `cube-root` and `sqrt` are actually the exact same procedure once average damping is applied
Because `fixed-point` automatically detects whether a cube root or square root is wanted from the initial guess
Because average damping only works for square roots, so `cube-root` needs an entirely different algorithm built from scratch
questions.explanation: Both are instances of the same idea - find a fixed point of an average-damped transform - differing only in which function of y is damped (x/y vs x/y^2), which is exactly the reusable structure the text is showcasing.

questions.prompt: How does the `deriv` procedure approximate the derivative of a function `g` at a point `x`?
options: By computing (g(x+dx) - g(x)) / dx for a small constant dx
By symbolically differentiating the body of g using algebraic rules
By calling g twice at x and dividing the two results
By repeatedly averaging g(x) with itself until it stabilizes
questions.explanation: deriv implements the standard finite-difference approximation to a derivative - the change in g's output over a tiny step dx in its input - rather than any kind of symbolic differentiation.

questions.prompt: How does `newtons-method` use `fixed-point` to find a zero of a function `g`?
options: It calls `fixed-point` on `newton-transform` applied to g, i.e. on the function x -> x - g(x)/Dg(x), since a fixed point of that transform is a zero of g
It calls `fixed-point` directly on g itself, since any fixed point of g is automatically a zero of g
It repeatedly averages g(x) with x until the average stops changing
It calls `deriv` on g and then treats the derivative's own zero as the answer
questions.explanation: The chain is: newton-transform builds x -> x - g(x)/Dg(x) using deriv; newtons-method just runs fixed-point on that transformed function, since finding where the transform stabilizes is mathematically the same as finding where g is zero.

questions.prompt: What do the two `sqrt` procedures built from `fixed-point-of-transform` (one passing `average-damp`, one passing `newton-transform`) have in common?
options: Both call the same general procedure, `fixed-point-of-transform`, differing only in which transform procedure they pass alongside the function and initial guess
Both compute the derivative of x -> x^2 - y explicitly before searching for a fixed point
Both are restricted to work only for square roots and cannot be reused for any other computation
Both bypass `fixed-point` entirely and use a closed-form formula instead
questions.explanation: fixed-point-of-transform factors out the shared shape - take a function g, transform it, find a fixed point of the result - so the two sqrt definitions are just two instantiations of that one general procedure with different transform arguments (average-damp vs newton-transform).

questions.prompt: What is the key point the text makes about procedures like `average-damp`, `deriv`, and `fixed-point-of-transform`?
options: They let a programmer name and manipulate whole general methods of computation, not just ordinary numeric values, extending the reach of procedural abstraction
They exist only to make code shorter, with no effect on what can be expressed
They are special forms built into the interpreter rather than ordinary procedures
They only work correctly in Scheme and can't be expressed in other higher-order-capable languages
questions.explanation: The text's closing point is that these higher-order procedures let general methods (like 'average damp this' or 'take the derivative of this') become explicit, nameable, manipulable elements of the language - not just a way to save keystrokes.

questions.prompt: According to the text, which of these is one of the 'rights and privileges' of a first-class element in a programming language?
options: It may be returned as the result of a procedure
It must always be a numeric value, never a procedure
It cannot be stored inside a data structure, only used directly
It can only be passed as an argument, never named by a variable
questions.explanation: The text lists four rights of first-class elements: being named by variables, passed as arguments, returned as results, and included in data structures; being returnable as a procedure's result is exactly one of these, and Lisp grants procedures all four.
